title: Fitbit Edge Announced: Everything You Need to Know!
content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

Fitbit has decided there will be no Fitbit Charge 7. Instead, the device will now be known as the Fitbit Edge, and with that, it follows more closely in line with the user interface of the Google Pixel Watch 5, alongside technology stashed inside the recent screenless Fitbit Air. If there were any questions as to whether or not Google remains committed to the Fitbit branding (in name), this would certainly answer that. Fitbit as a brand is clearly here to stay, even if they renamed the app to Google Health earlier this year.

The Fitbit Edge is a small-screen activity tracker, just like the Fitbit Charge series before it. With it, Google has made some big changes, mostly good, but not all good. On the ‘good’ side, they’re claiming the GPS is now actually functional. Previously, on the Fitbit Charge 5 & Charge 6, the GPS only worked if you loosened the band substantially, but when you did that, heart rate stopped working. For real. They even admitted it was a design choice at the time. Now, Fitbit is saying GPS should be “40% better” than the Charge 6. Plus, they added an altimeter, for both stair tracking and elevation tracking.

Beyond that, the Fitbit Edge gets all of the automatic workout recognition pieces of the Fitbit Air, except as of today, that sport list goes from like 10 sports to roughly 100 sports. Meaning even if you don’t press any buttons, it’ll still figure out that you’re pole dancing. Or…maybe that icon is a stand-up paddleboarder. It’s fuzzy. Atop that, the user interface now matches the Pixel Watch 5, which is cleaned up. Oh, and it’s got a ‘real’ button now, versus a touchable pseudo-button. But there are some downsides too – like no more Google Pay (contactless payments). And the price has significantly increased, up to $179USD from the usual $99-$129 that the Charge 6 floats at these days.

In any case, I’ve got a unit that I can start sharing hands-on details on tomorrow, but for now, here’s everything you need to know.

What’s New vs Charge 6:

The Fitbit Edge is the next version of the Fitbit Charge 6, which came out in 2023. Here’s how it’s different:

– Increased screen/display by 46% (has 1.34” display)
– Case thickness is 11.5mm
– Added physical side button that actually clicks (previous was just a touch area)
– Added altimeter (for stair tracking, as well as elevation tracking)
– Added automatic workout detection (now supports 100 sports)
– Increased supported manual workout profiles to 50 workout profiles
– Made user-replaceable/serviceable battery (the first Fitbit-branded product to do so)
– GPS accuracy improvement claimed at 40% more accurate (via new GPS chipset, and new aluminum case design)
– Switched to a more modern user interface, matching the Pixel Watch 5 series
– Added structured workout support
– Added support for dual usage with Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air (e.g., switching back and forth seamlessly)
– Added fast charging (5 minutes gets you 1 day of usage)
– Removed Google Pay (NFC Contactless payments)
– Removed EDA Scan feature (but does have continuous stress monitoring in the background)
– Changed the band attachment mechanism (old Fitbit habits die hard)
– Switched the charger to the same charger as the Fitbit Air (hey, at least they picked something else they already had this time)
– Added a bunch of band accessory types
– Price increased to $179 (officially the Charge 6 was $159 previously, but realistically it sat between $99 and $129 virtually all the time)
– Also a Stephen Curry model at $219 (US, Canada, EMEA)
– Pre-orders start today; availability October 27th.

In terms of some other general specs, just for recap purposes:

– Same claimed 7-day battery life
– Still has heart rate broadcasting feature via Bluetooth (though it can be a bit funky in terms of compatibility)
– Still has music control of your phone’s music (no onboard music storage)
– Still has Google Maps turn-by-turn directions (with phone)
– Still has smartphone notifications (more integration on Android than iOS)
– Still has full sleep tracking
– Still has continuous heart rate monitoring (background and workout)
– Still supports high & low heart rate alerts
– Supports the Google Health Guardian features announced a few months ago
– You can do quick replies on Android, though not on iOS devices
– Has FDA/EU approved medical ECG functionality, including background Afib detection
– Includes skin temperature sensor
– Supports Steps, Distance, Active Zone Minutes, VO2Max, Floor/elevation, Cardio Load, and many more metrics
– Two sizes of bands (see specs below)
– Water resistance level is 5ATM, and IP68 for dust protection

Finally, for lack of anywhere else to stick it, Google also announced a multi-year partnership with Flo Health (which has 80 million users), which will allow bidirectional syncing of data between the two platforms starting early next year. From Flo Health to Google Health, you’ll be able to pull your cycle data in. And then from Google Health to Flo Health, you’ll be able to send resting heart rate, skin temperature, heart rate variability, and sleep metrics. Further, on the Google Health side, it’ll leverage your cycle-tracking information for both general suggestions as well as workout suggestions. Finally, Google also noted:

“We will partner to build new products that are specifically designed for women, with a deep integration of Flo’s women’s health insights and algorithms with our expertise in wearable hardware and advanced sensors.”

It’ll be interesting to see if that’s hardware products or software “products”. Further, they noted there are upcoming plans around dedicated women’s health research initiatives (I assume that means large-scale studies you could opt-in to). Note that in the case of the Flo Health integration, Google says this is all optional, of course, and you can enable and then subsequently turn on/off things as you see fit.

Again, I’ll have much more hands-on details coming, starting tomorrow, but for now, let’s get to all the model options.

Detailed Tech & Model Specs:

The Fitbit Air case comes in 5 different colorways, and then with that there are approximately 2,328 band options. Starting off with the core options you can buy, they are as follows:

– Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band
– Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band
– Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Stephen Curry Special Edition

Finally, looking at the tech specs, here’s a whole slate of things that may or may not be interesting to you:

– Display is 1.34”/34mm AMOLED display, supporting an always-on configuration
– Display supports adjustable brightness
– Bluetooth 5.4
– Processor: Ambiq AP5 MCU
– GPS chipset supports GPS+Galileo in US, and GPS+Galileo+GLONASS+BeiDou+QZSS outside of US
– Onboard memory: 64MB NOR flash memory, 7 days of detailed motion data (minute intervals), 30 days of daily totals, heart rate at 2-second intervals
– Internal sensors: Altimeter, Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Red and infrared sensors for oxygen saturation (SpO2), Multipurpose electrical sensors compatible with ECG app, Photoplethysmography (PPG) optical heart rate sensor, Ambient light sensor, Far-field skin temperature sensor
– Battery is 65mAh
– Fully end-user replaceable battery
– Charging speed: 5 minutes of fast charging for 1 day of battery life, or 100% in 90 minutes
– Requires iOS 16.4 or newer, and Android 11 or newer
– Fitbit Edge Weight: 17.7g without band
– Fitbit Edge Dimensions: 39.22 x 25.56 mm
– Fitbit Edge Height/Thickness: 11.58mm
– Case is made from 100% recycled aluminum
– Active band: Silicone with “soft-touch coating”
– Active Band Sizing: Small fits wrists 130-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band: “Recycled polyester yarns with water-repellent coating and stainless steel lugs, as well as a raised interior print for increased airflow.”
– Stephen Curry band sizing (US): Small fits wrists 135-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band sizing (EU/Canada): Single-size fits wrists 150-195mm around
– Water resistance: 5ATM/50 meters
– Dust immersion resistance: IP68

I do want to point out that I’d love to have been a fly on the wall in conference rooms at Google when they debated putting the ‘Hoeing’ activity type in there. I just can’t wait for the Instagram meme jokes that come from that.

(As a geeky aside, it’s astonishing how detailed/comprehensive Google/Fitbit has become with their technical information, imagery, videos, and detailed documents explaining things. While I get full briefings, devices sent on time, and seemingly 24×7 responses within minutes, even on holiday weekends, it’s just such a difference to what some companies do, where every question is almost begging for answers. When companies make it easy to cover your products, you’ll find media tend to cover it with more details.)

Some Fitbit Air Updates:

As part of all of this, the Fitbit Air gets a few quite notable updates. First and the biggest is a massive expansion of the automatic workout detection profiles, from roughly 10 (though realistically it was less than that), to 100 sport profiles. I don’t yet have an official text listing of those profiles, though here is a nifty screenshot of all the icons that are included in this listing:

At present, I can only assume that the one with the person holding onto the pole is pole dancing. Sure, some might argue SUP. But what’s the fun in that? I’ll update this once I have a full listing. [Update: Just added in full list above. No pole dancing…but hey, there’s ‘Hoeing’.]

Do note that Fitbit says some of this is coming from understanding your patterns, rather than straight sport recognition. When it comes to automatic workout detection, there’s sorta two levels. The first is the device/platform (most processing is done in the cloud) actually being able to figure out that you were running, or cycling, or mountain biking. That’s the most ideal scenario. The second level is when a platform knows that you did something, but is a bit fuzzy on what exactly. In those cases, they can look at your history and context and say “Oh, every Saturday morning she goes mountain biking and she updated past activities to specify that, so this must be mountain biking because it’s Saturday morning”. That’s so-so in my opinion, because it’s better than nothing, but still not really nailing the movement recognition as good as Whoop does.

Nonetheless, Fitbit says that with this new algorithm they are “2x more accurate” in detections, and reduced “missed workouts by more than half”. Workouts must still meet the minimum 15-minute threshold as in the past.

Next, there are some new Metal Mesh bands coming out for the Fitbit Air. This includes a Champagne Gold or Polished Silver band for $69, or you can buy the Champagne Gold band with a Fitbit Air for $149 (so basically a $20 savings). Here’s what that looks like:

And here’s the polished silver one:

And finally, as previously announced, the Health Guardian feature will start unlocking reports later this month for existing Fitbit Air users, as well as other Fitbit users.

Once the firmware rolls out for the Fitbit Air and the new sport profiles, I’ll start digging into it and report back.

Going Forward:

Now, starting tomorrow, I can start sharing details from the device itself. Of course, having such lineage to both the Fitbit Charge 6 and their more recent products like the Fitbit Air & Pixel Watch 5, I don’t really expect any sort of crazy surprises here. However, the sport mode expansions are real and quite legit. Up to 100 sports now in auto-detect mode for both Fitbit Air & Fitbit Edge is a huge shift, and now much more competitive with Whoop (at least in theory; we’ll have to see in reality).

While the unit is priced higher, I think some of the added features may make it worthwhile. Notably, the structured workouts support, added altimeter for stairs/elevation, the theoretical improvements in GPS accuracy, plus the bigger display. Of course, the removal of Google Wallet/Pay seems like an odd choice to me. In this scenario, especially for iPhone users, it’s not really pushing those users up to the Google Pixel Watch, because that doesn’t work for iOS (just Android). Perhaps eventually Google will unlock the Pixel Watch for iOS users too.

In any case, plenty more to come shortly on the Fitbit Edge as I dive into testing.

With that, thanks for reading!
